utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say the Brigadier. I beg his pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, thank you for coming back. You remain, of course, under the solemn declaration which you took before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I know you predicted three hours yesterday. Perhaps you could try and improve on that. See if we can get through the witness today, because we've got a lot of business tomorrow to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is no way that I will be able to be completed with the witness today, I regret to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, during your tour you had the chance to sit down with the military leaders from the Muslim forces and have a frank discussion with them regarding their military objectives, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They confided to you, in fact, that their strategic plan was to slice up the Vitez-Busovaca enclave into a number of discrete pieces; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been -- yes, that was an efficient way of doing it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They were completely confident of their ability to do so, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were overconfident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, throughout your tour, sir, which lasted, I think we agreed in the last session that you were here, seven months?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout your tour they repeatedly attempted to achieve this objective, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I think in the last two months of my time there they had begun to realise that this task was beyond them, and they therefore stopped such determined attacks, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the military leaders with whom you met fairly frequently, sir, I believe, was General Mehmed Alagic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He is a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with General Alagic his plans with respect to the position of the Muslims in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long-term aim of the BiH forces to, if you like, liberate the Muslims of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Alagic had actually published a book about the war in Central Bosnia in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you a section from page 26. I would like to ask you whether these options and the decision was discussed with you. He says: "I was concerned by a specific issue, what to do with the civilians if we entered Vitez. Should we create conditions for their surrender? Or the second option was to allow their movement to the south-west. The third option was to keep them besieged and pressured so that our supplies from Croatia would not be completely withheld. Faced with this overall situation, we chose the last option. Instead of liberating Vitez, we chose to leave it as a strategic vent for supplying of other parts of Bosnia." Did General Alagic ever express those views to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did. The three options were expressed. We discussed them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the next page of his book, General Alagic says: "Through connections in the U.N., we succeeded in getting some ammunitions, weapons into Stari Vitez so that they could defend themselves."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware he put that in the book. You've made me aware. He would use every effort he could to get weapons, ammunition and food into that pocket. Whether he achieved that or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And just to conclude this line of questions regarding General Alagic, do you recall meeting with General Alagic on the 6th of November, 1993, just before you had lunch with the Croat leaders?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think that's in my diary, the extract which you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, why don't we make this an exhibit. Mr. President, I will say that there are no entries here of a personal nature, and I appreciate the Brigadier making these available. The entries in this diary are all relevant to the events in this case. So I don't believe that there would be any personal embarrassment factor through making these a public exhibit, unless the Brigadier objects to that.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's what you've asked me to do and I've expunged the bits that I believe were personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D133/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just ask you to turn to the last page of this exhibit, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Place it on the ELMO, please, for the interpreters. Could the document be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If we could put this on the ELMO. I have highlighted the portions with the significant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but have you got copies for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I regret to say that we do not have those copies with us today, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, some seem to have gone. But over the adjournment we ought to make sure that there are copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Meanwhile the interpreters should have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's my fault and I apologise to the Court and to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I meant to say "should have." They are getting them. They are in fact getting the copies. So there is no need to put them on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, the references to Enver, Dzemo and Mehmed are all -- those are all first names or diminutives, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enver Hadzihasanovic, Dzemal Merdan and Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These gentlemen communicated to you that there was a party line that they were prepared to follow to the letter, and that was that the war would go on as long as necessary to secure to the Muslim side, if you will, their territorial gains; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they stated at that stage. They told me a lot of things over the seven months, some of which came to pass, a lot which didn't come to pass, a lot which were good ideas, and a lot which I -- in many cases they perhaps wanted me to know, or not, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that one of the things that you were told was that there were plans to shell the HVO headquarters at the Hotel Vitez at approximately 5 p.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said I was going to lunch that afternoon with Blaskic and others, as a farewell lunch, and Alagic said, "You had better be out by 5.00." The locations weren't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the last entry in your diary on that day, I take it, refers to that: "The lunch went on a bit long. The result was that the shells that Alagic had promised came into the hotel area. Someone was wounded, as we heard the screams." And you conclude with the observation that "Alagic will, of course, think the whole thing is hilariously funny."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall, on the subject of Stari Vitez, Brigadier, a proposal that was made early on in your tour, communicated, I believe, to Major Roy Hunter, through Pero Skopljak, and that this proposal involved permitting the troops or the Muslims in Stari Vitez to leave Stari Vitez, provided that they surrendered their weapons to UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't honestly remember that proposal directly. It is -- it is quite a reasonable proposal to make. Whether the Muslims or the HVO or anyone would agree with that, I don't know, but it is not an unreasonable proposal to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can jog your memory further. As part of this proposal, the HVO government in Vitez would guarantee the safety of the Muslim civilians in Stari Vitez, and the forces in Stari Vitez, the Muslim forces, actually turned down that proposal; does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible. A not unreasonable assumption. The track record, that far, of HVO forces guaranteeing Muslims safety was not terribly good in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall incidents where -- well, actually, let me rephrase the question: You testified, I believe, with respect to the killing of a UNHCR driver by the name of Boris, and I believe that that was August the 14th, 1993, as we had stipulated; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall that ten days later, a UNHCR convoy actually made it into Stari Vitez; lorries with supplies, humanitarian aid, were permitted to enter Stari Vitez. The lorries were unloaded, and as soon as they left, the ABiH started blazing away at the Croat-held part of town and the convoy? Perhaps I can jog your memory, if the usher would be good enough to show you Z1179, which is a copy of milinfosum 117, sir, dated August the 24th, 1993. The entry to which I would like to draw your attention is a very short one. It's a paragraph numbered 3, just under the "Vitez" entry. Does that jog your memory, or do you have no recollection of that particular event, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that -- yes, yes, I recollect it now, having seen the milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Brigadier. I've finished with that. Let's just move on quickly to another subject, since time is precious here, if we can.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just ask if you are making the insinuation that a UNHCR convoy which I was responsible for escorting had taken weapons into Stari Vitez? If you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- making that insinuation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, there is no question, sir, that the protection and control of main supply routes is an overriding, important, and legitimate goal in an infantry war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you would agree that it's militarily necessary to defend main supply routes to the maximum extent of the power and ability of the forces having those supply routes under their control; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In balance; you would have to keep it in balance. You would need to establish and maintain main supply routes, with alternatives, in case they were blocked. And you would adjust -- obviously adjust your main supply routes as battle goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's a certain amount of fluidity in any kind of a warfare situation with the ebb and flow of the military advantage between forces; wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in order to control main supply routes, especially in areas such as Central Bosnia, which consist of deep valleys and ravines and so forth, you would agree that it would be vital to control any high ground adjacent to the main supply route as an adjunct to the overriding military objective of ensuring that the main supply route remains under your control; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would make an appreciation as to the best way of protecting that main supply route. That may in some cases mean picketing the high ground; in other cases it may not. It's a question of the level of the threat, the terrain, and a number of other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But generally speaking, if high ground can be captured by opposing forces, from which they can fire down onto troops using the main supply route for reinforcement, for example, or aid moving back and forth, there is no question that the protection or capture of high ground overlooking the main supply route is a reasonable and legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a legitimate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters appeal to counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a legitimate objective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you would agree, sir -- I don't think there's any doubt about this -- that the key to the defence of the entire Vitez/Busovaca pocket was the main supply route that ran up from Novi Travnik, through Vitez, along to Kaonik, and down through Busovaca; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key to the defence of Vitez was the ability to move from -- quickly and rapidly across the pockets. Whether that was on a main supply route or on an alternative doesn't matter; it's the ability to move, and not the main supply route, that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was just picking up, sir, on a statement that you made on page 4 of the statement you gave to the investigators working for the Prosecution on the 12th of August, 1996, and the 16th of April, 1997. I don't think there is any dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, may I interrupt here on a matter. This is not the first time you've put to a witness a question beginning "Do you agree that." The witness then says he either does agree, or often he qualifies what he's said. You then produce his statement and contradict him. Now, we are dealing with events here which lasted a very long time ago -- took place a very long time ago. We are dealing with statements which witnesses gave a long time ago, four or five years ago, and I don't think it's fair to expect them to remember precisely what is in their statements, even if they have been able to refresh their memory from it. If you want to put something from a statement to a witness, the fair way to put it is to read out what he said in the statement and then say, "That's what you said; do you agree with that still," rather than the other way around, which I'm sure you don't intend it, but looks as though it's a trick or a trap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was not intended to be, Mr. President. I'm grateful for the guidance, and I will do exactly as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 4 of the statement that you gave to the investigators two and a half years ago, sir, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- "... Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're going too fast for the interpreters. Could you read that out again, so I can just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- catch the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It says: "The key to the Defence of the Vitez pocket was the main road, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, and I was -- I believe that my statement goes on at that stage to describe how the Vitez pocket was defended. It may not have been in that particular part of my statement, but I did describe in some detail the method, very similar to the First World War, how the Vitez pocket was defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few final questions in this regard. When your tour began and when it ended, the Croats had essentially been squeezed into geographically isolated enclaves; that's fair to say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- during the -- they were quite dominant in the Vitez area when I first arrived, but during the course of my seven months, they were indeed squeezed into a number of pockets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that the Vitez/Busovaca pocket was a vital area for the Croats for a number of reasons, including the location of the armaments factory or the explosives factory in Vitez itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've already been over the offensive launched in June of 1993, and I don't believe it would be necessary to revisit that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Addressing your attention, Brigadier, to a separate subject, which is the military chain of command of the HVO, you were aware that the supreme commander of the HVO forces was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you were also aware that the chief of the HVO general staff in Mostar was Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic reported directly to Brigadier Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in your view, operational command of all HVO forces in Central Bosnia was exercised directly from the Hotel Vitez, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational command for the defence of the pocket, using the troops, yes, was exercised from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a former battalion commander yourself, you viewed yourself, in that capacity, as having sole responsibility for the actions of troops under your command, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given that formal authority by the commander of the British forces in former Yugoslavia who was based in Split, who had delineated my boundaries and those people under my command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's a fairly normal situation for a battalion commander, isn't it, to have sole responsibility for the actions of the troops under your command?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there can also be other people stationed in your area who you're not -- you have no action -- it's to do with command states. There are a number of varying command states in most forces which describe those forces directly under those command, those in location, those in locations you have some authority over, and those in locations you might be providing administrative support for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just suggest to you that you testified on page 9040 of the Blaskic case as follows: that you were in "sole responsibility for all of the actions of the troops under my command, which is quite normal. That was absolutely standard practice. There is one commander, who is directly responsible for all actions of his troops, good or bad." Do you still subscribe to that view today, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but it again depends on the command status. I was given that authority. It is not always given to everybody. It is not a standard argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say that with a few minor exceptions, Brigadier, you viewed the HVO as similar to any modern professional army in the world?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I've stated that their organisation, with particular reference to their territorial organisation, was the same as any modern army in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The HVO, as far as you were aware -- and I think it's been exhibited -- had a full code of military discipline, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, the HVO had established military courts and also a district military prosecutor's office; you were aware of that, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I have referred to it on a number of occasions, when I've stated that I -- well, I knew that something had happened; I couldn't actually prove it had happened, but they -- soldiers had been through jurisdiction. And I also stated on a number of occasions that the HVO in the Vitez pocket, in their command structure, had a different command structure to the BiH, with this political element at the top. And that has been produced, I believe, as an exhibit in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You viewed the existence of a detailed code of military discipline, the existence of military courts, and a military prosecutor, as the sign of a developed army with a good command structure, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part of the structure of a developed army, yes. Provided those courts are used. I mean, anyone can produce a structure and a code. If the code is used and followed, that's fine. Just because standing institutions are in place, doesn't mean that the right practices are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just draw your attention to page 9106 of your testimony against General Blaskic. You testified as follows: "I was aware that there was a full code of military discipline backing up the HVO, as published, I believe, by the government of Herceg-Bosnia, which details right down to the detail of how to deal with court cases and process for disciplining. That is a sign of a developed army that has a good command structure." And you agree with that today as well, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that. But I must go back to my reply to your previous question. Even if the code is in place, it doesn't necessarily have to be used. And you will recall -- if I could, sir, be allowed to mention that on the 8th of September, I think -- wrong. I'll reclarify. After the convoy came through, when I spoke to Kordic, one of the agreements he made was that he would investigate the deaths of the eight people who were killed. No such investigation took place. Now we are saying there is a code there for military forces, and the areas under martial law, and no such investigation took place. That would imply to me that the code wasn't being followed. At other occasions the code was followed. When I asked Blaskic to investigate the arrival of a rocket in my camp, he dealt with that very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question in connection with the comment that you just made, Brigadier. Following the deaths of the eight drivers in the Convoy of Joy, which was a private convoy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Muslim convoy -- yes, it was not an UNHCR convoy, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever have any further written or oral communications with Mr. Kordic on that subject?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of asking for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I asked him the once. And he didn't follow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I mean, I could have badgered him at every meeting. In fact, we didn't meet very often after that, as you know. But there are other things to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what role politicians played in the process of military discipline within the HVO military forces, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know directly, but I would assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, there is no need to assume, sir. In the British army what role, if any, do civilian politicians play in the process of military investigations and military discipline? None, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's wrong, because every year parliament has to vote and clarify that we are allowed to keep our army. And in doing so it then endorses the Army Act in the U.K., and we are allowed to carry on soldiering for another year. Without that vote, there is no authority for anything in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. I understand that, Brigadier. The point I make is slightly different, and that is this: Once a military investigation has been initiated, in the British army civilian politicians don't play any role whatsoever in that investigation or in the process of court martial or military prosecution; wouldn't that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a -- no, there is an organisation sitting on top of the court martial process, which ensures and audits all the trials that have taken place, to make sure that they are acceptable within military law and complying with civil law, and we don't exceed any of our boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Once again, let me just ask you. With respect to -- and I don't mean to badger you, but I would like an answer to this question. With respect to a regular investigation of a particular crime, military crime, that is the subject of a court martial, it's true, is it not, that civilian politicians in your system, in the British army, play absolutely no role whatsoever in the Prosecution or investigation of the crime?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the -- I don't wish to evade this. It does depend on the level of the crime. If a soldier is caught drunk, he may well be dealt with at the appropriate level. If he is caught committing a murder, that will then escalate the level at which it can be dealt with, and it certainly couldn't be a commanding officer. It would then go to a court martial. If it goes to a court martial, there is a judge advocate general who sits on that, who is not a military person. He is civilian. And he is there to see we do our business again correctly. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No more questions on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the point is made, Your Honour, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the rules of military discipline about which you testified, I think that it was Exhibit Z200,1. I wonder if the usher would give you a copy of that. Do you have before you the English version of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Military discipline. All right. Let me just go through some of these fairly lengthy provisions with you in an expeditious way. Could you just turn to Article 16.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were aware that the Supreme Commander of the HZHB armed forces, Mr. Boban, as you previously testified, if so requested or proposed, could reduce, mitigate or remit disciplinary measures of punishment. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. You have made me aware of the sentence now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please. The interpreters do not have copies of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many of these Articles do you want to go through?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Probably four, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you just refer us to them without --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will do precisely that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because the interpreters don't have copies and it's much more difficult for them. What's the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For the Court's information, I would just draw the attention to Article 51, which provides that: "Disciplinary offences shall be tried by the general staff's military disciplinary courts of first instance and superior military disciplinary courts." The only question that I wanted to ask the Brigadier in that regard was this: Were you aware that there was a two-tier system of courts within the HZHB: military disciplinary courts of first instance and superior military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very similar to the system -- to the one we have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Article 54 provides that military disciplinary court trials shall be conducted by a three-judge council, with one presiding judge. Is that similar to the system that's in place in your armed forces, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems quite reasonable, and it's very similar to most armed forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the final provision to which I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention is Article 95, which provides to whom the presidents of the inferior and superior Tribunals shall be accountable. "The President of the first-instance military disciplinary court and the prosecutor bear disciplinary liability for their work in court and answer to the chief of the general staff or commander of the operative zone, where the military disciplinary court is located." Were you aware of that provision, sir, or are you looking at it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am looking at it in detail for the first time. Am I permitted to ask a question at this stage, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not normally, but on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have a -- this is fine, looking through all these Articles, but there's a basic premise in the British military, is whether that the crime is a military crime or a civilian crime. And very often the civilian authorities may claim jurisdiction and take it off the military. It depends on the nature of the crime. I believe that's common to most countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Brigadier. But that never happened here, did it, with respect to, for example, the Ahmici investigation about which you gave testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second part of Article 95, Mr. President, to which I want to draw the Court's attention, is that: "The President of the superior military disciplinary court and the prosecutor shall bear disciplinary liability for their work in court and answer to the head of the Defence Department." Now, sir, do you know who the head of the Defence Department was of the HZHB, or the Republic, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia, when you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just turn to a separate subject, and that is the opinions you gave regarding some units of the military police. I wonder if the usher would show you first Exhibit Z881,1, which is a milinfosum number 35 dated June the 3rd, 1993, and about which you gave testimony in direct examination. The page to which I would like to draw your attention is the second page. Now, this is a milinfosum dated June the 3rd, even though it appears to be dated May the 3rd of 1993. I think you clarified that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was the Vitez LO at the time of this milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have either been Captain Angus Hay or Captain Lee Whitworth, one of the two. They took over. I'm not entirely -- my memory can't remember when they took over. But one of those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is a reference here to the 4th Battalion HVO MP, meaning, I take it, military police, AKA Jokeri, and then in brackets "Black Knights." Were you aware that the Croatian for Black Knights is Crni Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the town of Vitez means knight, yes. I mean, the extrapolation of that would be to do with knights, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are aware, I take it, that there is a separate detachment of special forces known as the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Whose comment appears in this milinfosum? Is that the comment of the military information officer himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The intelligence officer Captain Harrison, is my note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Captain Simon Harrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede, sir, that there was doubt, as of the date of this milinfosum, June 3rd, 1993, as to whether the control of the Jokeri or the 4th Battalion of the military police came under the direct control of Mr. Kordic, wouldn't you, and apparently it indicates that there is doubt on that subject; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't mean it's 100 per cent confirmed, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Absolutely. And once again the comment says that if this is the case, then it would confirm that Mr. Kordic would be senior in status to Blaskic and that the HDZ controlled the HVO. So that was still an open question at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a comment, as we've said, from Captain Harrison based on the information he received. And I would assume he would have added it to information he had also received in the past, in gaining a body of evidence, if you like, about the various organisations and command structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And thank you for pointing that out. I think that it's clear that these milinfosum, while they represent a snapshot in time, if you like, when put together show the evolution of BritBat's knowledge of what was going on on the ground, with the politicians, with the military. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If we could -- the next milinfosum I would like to show to you is in a different format. And I apologise; I only have a snippet of it. It's August the 8th, 1993. And if I could show it to you. And there are sufficient for the translators, my colleagues point out, Mr. President. This milinfosum appears to contain some further information regarding the Vitezovi. Apparently this organisation, at least according to the relator, Borislav Jozic, was controlled by Mostar and was commanded by one Bruno Stojic. Did you ever have any conversations with your military information officer or liaison officers on this particular subject, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the inference is made by Borislav Jozic, the statement as described here. Yes, we would have discussed it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Jozic, unfortunately, was killed in -- later in August of 1993; isn't that true? Shot by an ABiH sniper?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this staff officer in the headquarters of General Blaskic's office denied that the Vitezovi worked to Dario Kordic's direction. You were aware of that particular piece of information as of the date of this milinfosum in August of 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, I mean, that doesn't make the statement true or false. That was made by that staff officer. It's merely a statement that was made and recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document marked D134/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the final military information summary, milinfosum, that I would like to show to you in this regard, sir, is dated August the 10th, two days later. Thank you. It's military information summary 103.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D135/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The particular part that I would like to draw to your attention appears on page 5 of this document, sir, under the heading of orbats. And apparently the PWO liaison officer, or whoever was the source of the information upon which the military information officer relied, finally confirmed that the Jokeri and the Vitezovi were different units; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he concluded at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your recollection of the organisational structure, that in fact those two units were completely separate units with different commanders?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just read through this again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that at that stage we believed that there were two separate organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the Jokers and the 4th Battalion of the military police, I suggest to you that the commander of that unit and of the military police in your area of responsibility was Pasko Ljubicic, with his headquarters in the Hotel Vitez. That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't recognise the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we will adjourn now. We will sit this afternoon until half past 4.00, in the hope that we can finish. We'll take a short break at some appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't aware that we would be sitting this afternoon. If we are, then I may be able to be finished with the Brigadier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I didn't imagine you were going to finish in half an hour. But perhaps you might in an hour and a half. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry we're late starting. There was a hold-up with a local demonstration. Now, Mr. Sayers, I have a note from the -- or had representations from the interpreters about speed. Now, I recognise the difficulty, because you're under pressure of time, not least from the Bench; but you won't be criticised for speaking slowly. So perhaps you can practice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It certainly makes a large difference knowing that we have the afternoon as well as the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, just to give you some notion of where this cross-examination is going, and the Trial Chamber too, there are four subjects that I would like to cover with you. The first is continuation of the discussion of the chain of command and your dealings with Colonel Blaskic in that regard; the second is your meeting or meetings with Mr. Valenta about which you testified; the third is the five meetings that you had with Mr. Kordic about which you have also testified; and then a short final subject will be the civil affairs office, Mr. Randy Rhodes, and the reports that he generated. So without further ado, let me start out into the first subject. You would agree, sir, that Colonel Blaskic was, like you, a professional soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I understood he had been a captain in the JNA before these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You knew that he was a graduate of the military academy in Belgrade, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He had a full education, as far as you were aware, in the rules and regulations of war?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in tactics, how to plan operations, how to conduct them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in your view, sir, his mission was to defend the Vitez pocket, the Vitez/Busovaca pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you are of the opinion that he did an effective job in that endeavour?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. He did an extremely effective job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You, yourself, sir, never had occasion to discuss the Geneva Conventions, or the rules and regulations of war, if you like, with Colonel Blaskic, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that you made the decision only to deal with the military leaders of Colonel Blaskic's status and not with his subordinate commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have already stated that we had established a hierarchy to deal -- so we didn't have duplication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it is also true that you met with Colonel Blaskic about once a week; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As -- as and when we could, but obviously it was difficult from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your view, sir, Colonel Blaskic exercised full and complete operational command of all of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia directly from his headquarters at the Hotel Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the senior military commander. I do not know the exact command status of all the units, and we have discussed and talked about the Orbat, Order of Battle diagram, before, where we showed those main units, those main brigade units, are under command, but are not the detail of the other units that would have been in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that on several occasions you actually took the opportunity to question Colonel Blaskic on the subject of whether he was in fact in command in the Operative Zone covering each of the isolated pockets about which we've spoken, and he confirmed to you, when you asked him specific questions on that subject, that he was indeed in command?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he always said he was the military commander of the Ops Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The point I'm making is that you took the opportunity to clarify with him that particular subject on several occasions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as to his status as a commander, as he described to you, it was quite clear to you that he was in fact very much the commander, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had -- he had the headquarters and the capability of commanding, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You testified at page 9061 in the Blaskic case about a year and a half ago, quote: "As for his status as a commander, it was quite clear to me that he was very much the commander." And that's what you are saying today as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, sir, he had all of the trappings of command: for example, a large headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well-equipped staff?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Deputy commanders, such as Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Franjo Nakic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And liaison officers, such as Mr. Gelic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gelic, yes, was the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, in your view, he was a capable and successful commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was not just your view; this view was shared by other people in your area of responsibility, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my -- within my command, that view was shared; but others, from other aid agencies, I can't speak for them, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said in the Blaskic case, just a few pages after the passage that I read to you, at page 9063, that "It was quite clear to me he was a commander exercising command, issuing orders, controlling events as and when required, in the classic style of any military commander operating a large headquarters." And I take it, Brigadier, that that remains your view today as well?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you also stated -- and I believe this will be the last subject on that -- the last question on that subject -- at page 9065, that: "In order to operate the defence of the Vitez-Busovaca pocket successfully, there must be one commander. Secondly, he must have everything in that area directly under his command. And he must have an adequate information and communication system in order to be able to operate that defence. I have to say that Commander Blaskic operated that defence superbly because he had all of those ingredients." And that also remains your view today, sir; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the command characteristics, if you like, which you saw yourself exhibited by Colonel Blaskic, was his power to sign ceasefire agreements without consulting anybody else; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he actually signed such a ceasefire agreement, I believe, on June the 19th, with General Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be uncertain of the date without seeing the agreement, but yes, there were joint signatures on a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On a related subject, sir, the subject of the investigation into the terrible events at Ahmici was raised, and you gave some testimony on that. You were aware that Colonel Blaskic had in fact initiated an investigation into the events at Ahmici, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that, one, an investigation had been initiated. I wasn't aware of how far it had got. And I think it was due to a report in May sometime, the 25th as a date that springs to mind, but I couldn't be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, did you have any discussions with Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart, the departing CO of the Cheshire Regiment, regarding communications back and forth between Colonel Blaskic and BritBat in connection with how that inquiry was to be structured?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no. All I had was the fact that an inquiry was going to take place. We had communications by fax and telephone at an early stage with Colonel Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just suggest to you these documents are already in evidence, and I don't think there is any necessity to belabour this, but Colonel Stewart sent a letter to Colonel Blaskic on the 22nd of April asking him to initiate an investigation. Were you aware that one day later Colonel Blaskic offered to convene a multi-lateral investigative commission consisting of the HVO forces, or representatives, ABiH representatives, and BritBat representatives as well?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't directly aware of that, but it would seem an entirely reasonable thing to do, to get to the bottom of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were present in the area when representatives from the United Nations Centre for Human Rights actually came into the area and performed an investigation into the events at Ahmici, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had a number of people came. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that the results of their investigations turned up four specific names of people believed to have been present at the Ahmici fighting on April the 16th of 1993, and that those names were subsequently put into a letter that was communicated to Jean-Pierre Thebault, the ECMM regional centre head in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware or did you have any discussions with Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart about the fact that a deliberate and conscious decision was made to withhold those names from Colonel Blaskic and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you have any discussions with Colonel Blaskic, after your first meeting with him, which I think you said was on May the 9th of 1993, did you have any other discussions with him regarding the progress of the investigation into the Ahmici events?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There tended to be a standard list of questions for most meetings, which after two or three I realised were pointless. And I think on one occasion we both agreed it was pointless, if we both sat down and made the same five demands. So I stopped asking. I had a responsibility to get the aid through the pocket. It was therefore in order to ease the wheels; there is no point in irritating people. And there comes a point where you ask question after question, and at that stage there was very little point in going on any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So would the answer to the question be that after May the 9th of 1993 you did not actually raise the events at Ahmici or the status of the investigation with Colonel Blaskic again?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me address this subject a little cautiously, Brigadier. Would it be fair to say that you and Colonel Blaskic had a tense, distrustful relationship, one of animosity and distrust?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are saying I disliked Colonel Blaskic, that would be wrong. If you are saying I liked Colonel Blaskic, that would also be wrong. But if you are implying that my personal feelings against anybody I dealt with in Bosnia at any time would cloud my judgement, then I would -- I would dispute that. And I dispute that because that is not the way the British army does it. That is not the way I command it. And having recently come from a military ethics conference, of which I submitted a paper, it's something that I think is immoral almost, to allow judgments like that to cloud decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You discussed an incident when a RPG 7-round or rocket-propelled grenade hit the BritBat base in Nova Bila, and that actually left you absolutely furious, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite a natural reaction to be extremely angry when somebody tries to kill one of your soldiers, when you are actually there to keep people alive as best you can by the provision of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's perfectly understandable, Brigadier, and you actually sent off a blistering complaint immediately to Colonel Blaskic once that round had hit your army base; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He sent off blistering complaints to me at regular intervals as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that at the end of your tour you reviewed Colonel Blaskic's conduct and concluded that he had demonstrated a pattern of failure to act when it deemed -- when he deemed it not to be in his own interest?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. I have some -- are you asking for my feelings about Colonel Blaskic or an estimation of his professional skills?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me go through here. I am just referring to page 9094, the testimony that you gave in the Blaskic case on June the 3rd of 1998. You said: "But when I look back, I see throughout these events a pattern of failure by Commander Blaskic to act when he deemed it was not in his own interest. He would act only if he saw it as a direct benefit." Does that remain your view today?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That does remain my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, Colonel Blaskic made statements to you that were, as you testified, I believe, on the same page, blatantly not true; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, so untrue as to be almost completely unbelievable?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- but I found over the seven months I was there, that whether it is a feature of that part of the world, but there was a certain naivete in threats and the way people did business. Some of the suggestions made were in some cases childly naive and rather foolish in the eyes of -- in my eyes and in my country's eyes. We got -- you got used to that. There was no point in going back and questioning it, because that would have been rude and it wouldn't have been very constructive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, along those lines, in your very first meeting with Colonel Blaskic on May the 9th of 1993, your conclusion was that the explanations that he offered for what had happened at Ahmici were plainly and completely, absolutely ludicrous, to use the words that you used on page 9056 of the transcript one and a half years ago; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I believe I also stated that it was Colonel Bob Stewart who was leading that meeting. And I was sitting in the back row and not making any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you concluded that the three reasons he came up with were ridiculous, to use your words?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, sir, to go one step further, it was your conclusion that Colonel Blaskic was deliberately lying to you in your very first meeting with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say evading the truth rather than deliberately lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 9057, sir, of the transcript of your testimony one and a half years ago, you said, in response to this question: "Brigadier, and pardon my directness in this question, did you conclude that the defendant was lying to you?" And the answer was: "Oh, yeah. There was no other conclusion. He was lying. And the problem was, it wasn't even a clever lie. It was very naive." That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I mean, that's what I have said over the last two replies, I hope, that it was a very naive reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And moving forward to the Dobrila Kolaba incident, and this is the only question I have on that: Your conversation with Colonel Blaskic in connection with the HVO investigation into that item resulted in conclusions that you found to be almost ludicrous, right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you concluded that he was telling you a complete lie. Not only was it a small lie, it was such a huge and elaborate lie, as you stated one and a half years ago on page 9079 of the transcript; right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Departing from this subject a little bit and getting back into the chain of command, sir, and the last set of questions on that. You were familiar with the fact that a joint operations command had been set up in early June of 1993, following the outbreak of the hostilities in April and the ceasefire agreements that, temporarily anyway, resolved those; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Travnik joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And that commission was established by order of Colonel Blaskic for the HVO and General Hadzihasanovic for the 3rd Corps in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, as the senior commanders, they would be responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as a result of that, there were a series of joint meetings held between senior Croat and Muslim military leaders in an attempt to try to defuse tension; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at which myself, the ECMM and UNHCR, and, where possible, the Red Cross and others, would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But one person was never present at any of those meetings, and that was Mr. Kordic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a meeting of the military people for a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, the military commanders issued a series of joint orders dealing with things such as forbidding the expulsion of citizens from their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of the meetings, I issued a record of the decisions taken, and then I asked them to issue, down their chain of command, similar orders, to make sure that the word was carried down to their commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, those orders were passed down the chain of command by both sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be passed down. I mean, I can't say that they got down to the lowest level; I have no knowledge of how far they went. On some occasions, I saw the published paper, which, when it was translated, gave that effect. But as to how effective they had been done, I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Other subjects addressed by these joint commands were things such as maintaining peace in the various communities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As well as controlling criminal elements in those communities; right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede, sir, that that was a pretty pervasive problem throughout your tour of duty in the area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a wonderful excuse, and I think everybody throughout Bosnia -- and I mean wider Bosnia -- used it. There were always criminal elements somewhere. It's a -- it was used by everybody consistently. The great criminal element; I'd like to find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But to be fair, those kinds of complaints you found to be routine on both sides, the HVO and the ABiH, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a -- it's a very convenient way of denying responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There were also joint orders issued dealing with the treatment of prisoners as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And my final question on this subject is, the joint commission was actually disbanded; it fell into complete disuse, if you like, following the ABiH offensive in Travnik in June of 1993. Isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's absolutely correct, yes. It collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We don't need to identify this order unless you wish to see it, but you actually issued an order which contained exactly that observation: As a result of recent offensive activities in the area, the joint commission should be disbanded because it was no longer serving any useful function?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequent to a meeting where one side failed to turn up, and I think it was the ABiH failed to turn up, it was quite apparent there were so many violations of all of the provisions that we were trying to work for that it was pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One thing I simply don't know, and I don't know whether any evidence has been adduced on this subject; I suspect not: Do you know whether any such joint commission was ever revived after June of 1993, during your tour?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been revived, I suspect, later on in '94, in the latter half of '94, when the country was -- the U.N. decided to have sectors, and at those sectors, the concept of the joint commission was revived, from the top to the bottom, in order to get both sides working together. When it worked, it's fine; but it relies on cooperation and understanding by both sides. If that trust and cooperation breaks down, it's very difficult to generate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if I have my history correct, that trust and cooperation did break down, and there were no joint commissions from the dissolution of the joint commission in Travnik and Vitez in June of 1993 up until the signature of the Washington Agreements in March of 1994; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair to say, and that was replaced by, if you like, a shuttle diplomacy at the various levels, trying to calm tensions. Not very successful, but we tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was Colonel Blaskic one of the shuttle diplomats, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was one of the people I used to go and see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me depart this subject and go into talking about Mr. Valenta, if I may. Did you ever discover what Mr. Valenta's actual political position was?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's recorded in the back of one of the milinfosums that's already been produced here as evidence. He was deputy, I think, for the Vitez area -- or head of the Vitez area HDZ. I wouldn't, off the top of my head, be able to tell exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just suggest to you -- and I appreciate that there's a confusion of acronyms and so forth, and it's sometimes difficult to keep one straight from the other, but in terms of the HVO, did you know that he was actually a vice-president of the HVO and had held that position since October the 17th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that sounds about right, yes, I would think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you know that the president of the HVO, who had held that position since August, I believe, of 1992, was Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name does not ring a bell. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And just contrasting his position a little bit with Mr. Kordic's, did you know that Mr. Kordic was never a president, or vice-president, or really an officer of the HVO, or held any office in the HVO, other than on the commission of personnel, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I wouldn't -- I mean, Mr. Kordic had influence. He may not have had an official position, but he had influence. He spoke to me on behalf of the Croat population of the pocket on one occasion. I mean, that is somebody who feels he has influence. He also appeared, I'm aware, a number of times on television in that pocket. He was a man we thought had influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your mind, sir, you actually placed Mr. Valenta hierarchically higher, if you like, than Mr. Kordic; you saw Mr. Kordic as really one level down from Mr. Valenta. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of -- I think I placed Mr. Valenta as the author of -- and the man with the ideas; but then the separate plans to initiate those ideas were put by Mr. Kordic. And then, as I said before, I believe that Colonel Blaskic was the one who provided the soldiers to initiate those plans. So the hierarchy, if you like, has gone from the concept to a plan and to putting it into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said in the Blaskic case a year and a half ago, page 9054, that "The doctrine was there by Anto Valenta. I assumed that Dario Kordic was a politician, the next level down." Is that still your view today?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I qualify that? I wouldn't say that Dario Kordic was following the direct orders, as it were, in a hierarchical -- it's not a military hierarchical structure. It's a political structure. It's to do with influence, and talking, and people playing various parts. I wouldn't say they were Number 1 and 2; they had influence in different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you did assume that Mr. Kordic was the next level down, so one could infer from that -- correct me if I'm wrong -- that he basically took direction from Mr. Valenta, in your view, or at least that was your conclusion a year and a half ago?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my conclusion a year and a half ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Valenta never tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon me, Mr. Sayers; I think that we need to clarify this situation for the benefit of the Chamber. I should like to address myself to Brigadier Duncan. In your view, was there a hierarchical relationship between Mr. Valenta and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe there was a hierarchical relationship. They were, if you like, working on different subjects within the same organisation. So they were -- there was left and right; one being concepts and one making the plans. I don't think anyone had primacy over the other. It is easy to draw a diagram and put them down in a neat little box, and that's what a military mind would try to do; but this was a political organisation, not a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you refer to the concept, to the idea being established by Mr. Valenta, what do you rely on to say that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rely on -- sir, I rely on the big -- the large briefing he gave to me very early on in my tour, I think it was on the 12th of May, when I went to the Hotel Vitez and he explained to me his book and the ideas in his book for how the country of Bosnia should be organised. And he explained that in some detail. That's why I thought he was the man with the ideas for the future of his country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigadier Duncan -- and this will be my last question -- I would like us to be quite clear on this, because we are all searching for the truth, which is why we are here. When you say the concept on the basis of that book, did you or any of your assistants or people on the ground have -- did they address you, did you address Mr. Valenta, when you had any strategic problem, to seek a solution with him?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I tasked my liaison officer in Vitez to see Mr. Valenta to do with some problems to do with the local area of telephones and -- and what I call internal matters, as a political man, and I think that Mr. Randy Rhodes would have had dealings with him later on, as my political adviser. We only talked, Mr. Valenta and I, on two or three occasions at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you address Mr. Valenta for problems connected to military actions or operations?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not at all. Not the military side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually had occasion to send a formal complaint about HVO activities at Trnovac on May the 31st, 1993, both to Mr. Valenta and to Colonel Blaskic, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well have been. I also recollect I sent a strongly worded message to Mr. Valenta because he complained about my choice of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the point I'm making is a complaint was made on a variety of topics, including some military topics, to Colonel Blaskic and to Mr. Valenta in June of 1993; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be true. I was not always entirely clear who to address complaints to, and therefore some of them you will see information copies and, if you like, action copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on a little. You gave some testimony concerning a book that was given to you by Mr. Valenta. He never tried to contend at any time to you, sir, that this book had been adopted as the official policy of the Croat political institutions, did he?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but when you -- as I've said, I think, on the record already, when you are briefed by what seemed to be a senior political figure in that area, within days of arrival, he takes the time and trouble to brief the commanding officer of the battalion there, who effectively is the senior United Nations person on the spot, he takes three hours of one morning to take me slowly through the ideas in that book, you have to ask yourself why. I mean, clearly he is not doing it out of benign interest; he wants me to understand his ideas in that book. And he must have a reason behind that; otherwise it would be wasting everybody's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, neither Colonel Blaskic nor Mr. Kordic ever intimated to you that that book in any way reflected the official position of the Croat political institutions, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, they didn't, no. But I wouldn't -- I wouldn't expect that the subject of the book would come under conversation, certainly with Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When we were discussing Mr. Valenta in your previous testimony, I asked you a question, which was whether you were aware that he had recently returned to Vitez. Did you know that he was actually a teacher in Vitez prior to moving his office to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know he was a teacher in Vitez, because we discussed at that time a problem he had with, I believe, another teacher, who was of a different religion, who had left -- who had left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And did Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart tell you that he did not even know that this gentleman existed prior to the time that Mr. Valenta apparently moved back from Travnik to Vitez towards the beginning of May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that Colonel Bob Stewart knew that Mr. Valenta actually existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. So there is no way that Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart would have been in a position to brief you regarding the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the evidence that we have relating to this meeting, sir. And I think that you have reviewed your -- the notes that you made on May the 13th of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you will find I submitted, I think, seven pages, which are -- the first items, which are the direct photocopies from my diary taken after those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the second source that we have consists of your typewritten diary?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this was done contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
